questions.topic: Venn diagram and tree diagram probabilities
questions.fig: A Venn diagram: a rectangle U with two overlapping circles, Cats and Dogs. 64 is in the overlap and 48 in Dogs only; Cats only and the outside are blank. Part (b) shows a tree diagram to finish: B and S, then M, W, F, then V and O (only the branches after B then M are drawn in full).

parts.q: A survey of 168 people was carried out. Participants were asked whether they owned a cat or a dog. Some of the results are recorded in the Venn diagram below. Of those surveyed, 19 people did not own either a cat or a dog. Complete the diagram.
parts.scheme: Cats only $= 168 - 19 - 64 - 48 = 37$, and 19 outside the circles. Correctly filled diagram without work: full credit.

idea.title: Venn diagrams
idea.text: Each region of a Venn diagram is a different group: in A only, in both, in B only, and in neither (outside the circles but inside the box). Every person is in exactly one region, so all the regions add up to the total.

steps.say: 19 people own neither, so 19 goes outside both circles but inside the rectangle.
All four regions add up to the 168 people surveyed. Take away the regions you know to find Cats only.
Write 37 in the Cats-only part. The diagram is complete: 37, 64, 48 and 19 outside.

parts.q: A person is chosen at random from those surveyed. What is the probability that the person owned both a cat and a dog?

idea.title: Probability of an event
idea.text: When every outcome is equally likely, P(event) = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes. A probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

steps.say: "Both a cat and a dog" is the overlap of the two circles: 64 people.
Divide by the total, 168. Simplify by dividing top and bottom by 8. The probability is 8/21.

parts.q: What percentage of the people surveyed owned one animal only? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

steps.say: One animal only means cats only or dogs only: the two parts of the circles that don't overlap.
Write it as a fraction of 168 and multiply by 100 to make a percentage. Round to one decimal place: 50.6%.

parts.tip: "Only one" leaves out the overlap: don't add the 64.

parts.q: Mandy wants to buy a ticket to the theatre. She can choose a ticket in the Balcony (B) or the Stalls (S). Mandy can go on Monday (M), Wednesday (W) or Friday (F). For an extra charge she can choose a VIP ticket (V) where she will meet the band or she can choose the show only (O). Complete the tree diagram below, and hence or otherwise, find the probability that Mandy chooses a VIP ticket on a Wednesday. You may assume that all choices are equally likely.
parts.scheme: Tree: B and S each branch to M, W, F, and each day branches to V and O. $BWV = \frac12 \times \frac13 \times \frac12 = \frac{1}{12}$, $SWV = \frac{1}{12}$, so $\frac{2}{12}$ or $\frac16$.

idea.title: Tree diagrams
idea.text: A tree shows events happening one after another. Each branch is one possible result, labelled with its probability. The branches from one point add up to 1. Multiply along a path to get the chance of that path; add paths when more than one path fits.

steps.say: Mandy makes three choices: seat (B or S), day (M, W or F), then ticket type (V or O). All choices are equally likely, so each seat is 1/2, each day 1/3 and each ticket type 1/2.
Finish the tree: both B and S split into M, W and F, and every day splits into V and O. That gives 2 × 3 × 2 = 12 outcomes.
Find the paths with Wednesday and VIP: B → W → V and S → W → V.
Multiply along each path, then add the two paths. The probability is 1/6.

parts.tip: Or count outcomes: 2 of the 12 equally likely outcomes fit, so 2/12 = 1/6.

questions.topic: Probability from data, independent births and expected frequency
questions.stem: According to the Central Statistics Office (CSO) there were 65 909 babies born in Ireland in 2015. Of these 32 290 were girls.
questions.fig: A table of the probability of being born on each day of the week, with Tuesday left blank.

parts.q: How many boys were born in Ireland in 2015?

steps.say: Every baby is a boy or a girl, so the boys are all the babies take away the girls.
Put in the numbers. 33 619 boys were born.

parts.q: Find the probability that a baby picked at random from those born in Ireland in 2015 is a boy. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.scheme: $P(B) = \frac{33\,619}{65\,909} = 0{\cdot}51$ (51·01%). The answer must be shown as a fraction first for partial credit.

idea.title: Probability of an event
idea.text: When every outcome is equally likely, P(event) = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes. A probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

steps.say: Probability = number of boys ÷ number of babies.
Divide and round to 2 decimal places. The probability is 0.51.

parts.q: Eight babies were born in Limerick’s Maternity Hospital on 1 May 2015. Use your answer to part (a)(ii) to find the probability that the first three babies born were boys. Give your answer correct to 4 decimal places.

idea.title: Independent events: multiply
idea.text: Independent means one result does not change the chances of the next. Then the chance of a whole list of results is the single chances multiplied together.

steps.say: Each birth is independent: one baby being a boy doesn't change the chance for the next baby. So multiply 0.51 three times.
Round to 4 decimal places: 0.1327.

parts.q: Find the probability that the third birth was the first girl born in the hospital that day. Give your answer correct to 4 decimal places.

answer.show: 0.1274 (0.1275 if you use the exact fractions)

steps.say: "The third birth was the first girl" means: boy, boy, then girl. The first two must not be girls.
A girl is "not a boy", so P(girl) = 1 − 0.51.
Multiply and round to 4 decimal places. The probability is 0.1274.

parts.tip: The scheme also accepts 0·1275, which you get using the exact fractions instead of 0·51.

parts.q: The table below shows the probability of being born on a particular day of the week. Complete the table.

idea.title: Probabilities add up to 1
idea.text: A baby is born on exactly one day of the week, so the seven probabilities must add up to 1. The missing one is 1 minus all the others.

steps.say: Add the six probabilities you know.
All seven must add to 1, so Tuesday is what's missing. Tuesday's probability is 0.16.

parts.q: In a particular week 1300 babies were born. Find the number of babies expected to be born on the Tuesday of that week.

idea.title: Expected frequency
idea.text: Expected number of times = number of tries × probability. It's what you'd expect on average, not a guarantee.

steps.say: Expected number = total × probability. From (c)(i), the probability of a Tuesday is 0.16.
16% of babies are born on a Tuesday, so expect 16% of the 1300. That is 208 babies.

questions.topic: Two dice: sample space and probabilities; OR probability
questions.fig: A two-way table of the totals for two dice: Die 1 (1 to 6) across the top, Die 2 (1 to 6) down the side. Six totals are missing: two in row 4, two in row 5 and two in row 6.

parts.q: An experiment consists of throwing two fair, standard, six-sided dice and recording the sum of the two numbers thrown. Some of the totals are shown in the table. Complete the table.
parts.scheme: Every cell = Die 1 + Die 2 (totals 2 to 12). Correct answers outside the box with no work: zero credit.

idea.title: Sample space for two dice
idea.text: Each outcome is a pair (Die 1, Die 2). The table has 6 × 6 = 36 cells, one for every pair, and with fair dice all 36 are equally likely.

steps.say: Each cell is the number at the top of its column (Die 1) plus the number at the start of its row (Die 2).
Fill in the six gaps.

parts.q: Find the probability of getting a total of 7 or 11.

idea.title: Probability of an event
idea.text: When every outcome is equally likely, P(event) = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes. A probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

steps.say: Count the 7s: there are 6 of them, in a diagonal line. Count the 11s: 2.
A total can't be 7 and 11 at the same time, so just add the counts. Divide by the 36 outcomes. The probability is 2/9.

parts.q: Find the probability of getting a total which is a prime number.

steps.say: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. The totals run from 2 to 12, and the primes among them are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.
Count how many times each one appears in the table.
Add them up and divide by 36. The probability is 5/12.

parts.tip: 1 is not a prime, and 9 is not prime (3 × 3).

parts.q: A car distributor sells Ford cars and Renault cars. It has 30 cars for sale on a particular day; 18 are Ford cars and 12 are Renault cars. 7 of the Ford cars are red and 4 of the Renault cars are red. One of the 30 cars is chosen at random. What is the probability that the car chosen is a Ford car or a car which is not red?

idea.title: OR: count the overlap once
idea.text: "A or B" means A, or B, or both. Add the two groups, then take away the overlap so nothing is counted twice: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

steps.say: Sort the 30 cars into a table. Ford: 7 red, so 18 − 7 = 11 not red. Renault: 4 red, so 12 − 4 = 8 not red.
"Ford or not red" is every Ford (18) plus the Renaults that are not red (8). The Fords that are not red are already inside the 18, so don't count them again.
Divide by the 30 cars. The probability is 13/15.

parts.tip: Quick check: the only cars that are neither Ford nor "not red" are the 4 red Renaults, and 30 − 4 = 26.

questions.topic: Arrangements of RAINBOW; spinner probabilities and expected value
questions.fig: A circular spinner with seven sectors of different sizes (R, O, Y, G, B, I, V), and a table of each sector's angle and cash prize. Only Yellow's probability (1/8) is filled in.

parts.q: Find the number of different arrangements that can be made using all the letters of the word RAINBOW. Each letter is used only once.

idea.title: Arrangements and n!
idea.text: To arrange different things in a row, fill the places one at a time. The first place can take any of the items, the next place one fewer, and so on down to 1. 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 is written 7! ("7 factorial").

steps.say: RAINBOW has 7 letters, all different. Fill 7 places: 7 options for the 1st, then 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.
Multiply. There are 5040 arrangements.

parts.q: Find the number of different 3-letter arrangements that can be made using the letters of the word RAINBOW. Each letter is used at most once.

steps.say: Only 3 places to fill, with 7 letters to choose from and no repeats.
Multiply. There are 210 three-letter arrangements.

parts.q: A game, called Rainbow, uses an unbiased circular spinner. The spinner has seven sectors coloured red (R), orange (O), yellow (Y), green (G), blue (B), indigo (I), and violet (V) as shown below. The table below shows the angle of each sector. It also shows the cash prize that a player wins if the spinner stops in that sector. Complete the “Probability” column of the table which shows the probability of the spinner coming to rest in each sector after one spin.

answer.show: Red 1/5, Orange 1/12, Yellow 1/8, Green 1/4, Blue 1/6, Indigo 1/20, Violet 1/8

parts.scheme: Probability = angle ÷ 360°: Red $\frac15$, Orange $\frac{1}{12}$, Yellow $\frac18$, Green $\frac14$, Blue $\frac16$, Indigo $\frac{1}{20}$, Violet $\frac18$.

idea.title: Probability on a spinner
idea.text: An unbiased spinner is equally likely to stop anywhere around the circle. So a sector's probability is the fraction of the full turn (360°) that it covers: angle ÷ 360.

steps.say: Check the rule with the one that's given: Yellow is 45° and 45/360 = 1/8. So each probability is the sector's angle ÷ 360.
Do the same for every colour and simplify.
Check: all seven probabilities add to 1.

parts.q: Find the expected value of the prize that a player wins if they play Rainbow.
parts.scheme: $E(X) = \sum xP(x) = 20(\frac15) + 60(\frac{1}{12}) + 24(\frac18) + 8(\frac14) + 42(\frac16) + 90(\frac{1}{20}) + 48(\frac18) = 4 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 7 + 4{\cdot}5 + 6 = €31{\cdot}50$. Expected values correct but not added: full credit −1.

idea.title: Expected value
idea.text: The expected value is the average result per go if you played many, many times. Multiply each result by its probability, then add them all up: E(x) = Σ x·P(x).

steps.say: Multiply each prize by its probability. A table keeps it tidy.
Add them all up. The expected prize is €31.50.

parts.tip: Don't stop at the seven products: they must be added to get the expected value.

questions.stem: In a population, the probability that a person has blue eyes is 0·7.

parts.q: One person is chosen at random from the population. What is the probability that this person does not have blue eyes?

idea.title: The "not" rule
idea.text: Something either happens or it doesn't, so the two probabilities add up to 1. P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

steps.say: A person either has blue eyes or doesn't, so the two probabilities add to 1.
Subtract the 0.7 from 1. The probability is 0.3.

parts.q: Two people are chosen at random. What is the probability that both have blue eyes?

idea.title: Independent events: multiply
idea.text: Independent means one result does not change the chances of the next. Then the chance of a whole list of results is the single chances multiplied together.

steps.say: The two people don't affect each other (they're independent), so multiply along the path blue, blue.
The probability that both have blue eyes is 0.49.

parts.q: Three people are chosen at random. What is the probability that exactly two of them have blue eyes?

idea.title: "Exactly" means count the orders
idea.text: When the question doesn't say which people, the result can happen in different orders. Find the probability of one order, then multiply by the number of orders.

steps.say: Exactly two blue means one person is not blue. That person could be the 1st, 2nd or 3rd: 3 orders.
Each order has the same probability: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.3.
There are 3 orders, so multiply by 3. The probability is 0.441.

parts.q: Four people are chosen at random, one after another. What is the probability that the fourth person of the four chosen is the only one to have blue eyes?

steps.say: Only the fourth has blue eyes: not, not, not, blue. The question says which person, so there is only one order this time.
Multiply. The probability is 0.0189.

parts.tip: No × 4 here: the question names the person (the fourth), so only one order counts.

questions.topic: Twister: outcomes from two spinners, AND and OR
questions.stem: The game “Twister” is played using two spinners and a mat with coloured spots. The two spinners needed for the game are shown below. Both consist of four equal sections. A player spins both spinners and must then place their selected hand/foot on the selected coloured spot on the game mat. The spinners below show the outcome Right Hand on a Yellow Spot.
questions.fig: Two spinners, each with four equal sections: one with Left Hand, Right Hand, Left Foot and Right Foot; the other with Yellow, Red, Blue and Green. The arrows point to Right Hand and Yellow.

parts.q: How many different possible outcomes are there in the game?
parts.scheme: $4 \times 4 = 16$, or list all 16 outcomes (RH Y, LH Y, RF Y, LF Y, RH R, ...). Answer given as a probability: zero credit.

idea.title: The fundamental principle of counting
idea.text: If you make several choices one after another, multiply the number of options for each choice. Every option for the first choice can go with every option for the second.

steps.say: Spinner 1 has 4 outcomes and spinner 2 has 4 colours. Every body part can go with every colour, so draw a two-way table.
Multiply (or count the cells). There are 16 possible outcomes.

parts.q: Kate spins each spinner once. What is the probability that she must use: her left foot?

idea.title: Probability of an event
idea.text: When every outcome is equally likely, P(event) = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes. A probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

steps.say: Left Foot is one whole row of the table: 4 of the 16 outcomes (any colour).
The probability is 1/4. (Or just use spinner 1: 1 section out of 4.)

parts.q: a red or yellow coloured spot?

steps.say: Red and Yellow are two whole columns: 8 of the 16 outcomes.
A spot can't be red and yellow at once, so nothing is counted twice. The probability is 1/2.

parts.q: Jack spins each spinner once. What is the probability that the outcome is: his right hand and a blue spot?

steps.say: "Right hand and blue" is just one cell of the table.
So the probability is 1/16. (Or multiply: the spinners are independent.)

parts.q: his right hand or a blue spot?

idea.title: OR: count the overlap once
idea.text: "A or B" means A, or B, or both. Add the two groups, then take away the overlap so nothing is counted twice: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

steps.say: Right Hand is a row of 4. Blue is a column of 4. They share one cell: right hand and blue.
Add the row and the column, then take away the shared cell so it is only counted once. The probability is 7/16.

parts.tip: Count the shaded cells to check: 7 out of 16.

questions.topic: Coconut shy probabilities; area and perimeter of a composite figure
questions.fig: Part (b): a figure ABCDE made of a large square ACDE standing on the diagonal [AC] of a smaller square ABCF (side 2 cm). The small square is tilted so that B points down; the dotted lines AF and FC are inside the large square.

parts.q: At a stall in a fun fair, the probability of knocking a coconut off its support is 0·34. What is the probability of not knocking a coconut off its support?

idea.title: The "not" rule
idea.text: Something either happens or it doesn't, so the two probabilities add up to 1. P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

steps.say: You either knock the coconut off or you don't, so the two probabilities add to 1.
Subtract 0.34 from 1. The probability of not knocking it off is 0.66.

parts.q: David is given three attempts to knock the coconut off its support. What is the probability that he knocks the coconut for the first time, on his third attempt? Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

idea.title: Independent events: multiply
idea.text: Independent means one result does not change the chances of the next. Then the chance of a whole list of results is the single chances multiplied together.

steps.say: "First time on the third attempt" means: miss, miss, then hit.
The attempts are independent, so multiply. Round to 3 decimal places: 0.148.

parts.q: The figure $ABCDE$ shown in the diagram consists of a large square $ACDE$ standing on the diagonal $[AC]$ of a smaller square $ABCF$. The smaller square has a side length of 2 cm. Find the area and perimeter of the figure $ABCDE$. Give your answer for the perimeter correct to two decimal places.

idea.title: Pythagoras for a diagonal
idea.text: In a right-angled triangle, (longest side)² = (side)² + (side)². A square's diagonal is the longest side of a right-angled triangle made from two sides of the square.

steps.say: AC is the diagonal of the small square. Triangle ABC has a right angle at B and two sides of 2 cm, so use Pythagoras.
AC is also a side of the large square. Area of a square = side × side.
Below AC is triangle ABC: half of the small square.
Add the two areas. The area is 10 cm².
The perimeter is the distance around the outside: AB, BC, CD, DE and EA. AC is inside the shape, so leave it out. Round to two decimal places: 12.49 cm.

parts.tip: Perimeter means only the outside edges. The diagonal AC is inside the figure.

questions.topic: Free throws: independent events; mean from a frequency table
questions.fig: Part (b): a table of the number of games in which Rohan scored 0, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 16 points.

parts.q: During a match, Rohan takes a number of free throws. He scores 70% of his free throws, on average. Assume that scoring his free throws are independent events. Find the probability that he scores his first 3 free throws.

idea.title: Independent events: multiply
idea.text: Independent means one result does not change the chances of the next. Then the chance of a whole list of results is the single chances multiplied together.

steps.say: He scores 70% of the time, so P(score) = 0.7 for each throw.
The throws are independent, so multiply three times. The probability is 0.343.

parts.q: Find the probability that he scores exactly 2 of his first 3 free throws.

steps.say: A miss has probability 1 − 0.7 = 0.3.
Exactly 2 scores means one miss, and the miss could be the 1st, 2nd or 3rd throw: 3 arrangements (SSF, SFS, FSS).
Each arrangement has probability 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.3. Multiply by 3. The probability is 0.441.

parts.tip: 0·147 on its own is only one arrangement: remember the × 3.

parts.q: Give one reason why scoring his free throws might not be independent events.

answer.show: His earlier throws may affect the next one: e.g. a miss can make him nervous, or a score can give him confidence.

parts.scheme: Previous performance levels may affect future performance. (Partial explanation: partial credit.)

steps.say: Independent means one throw's result doesn't change the chance of the next. So give a real reason why it could change.
Model answer: his previous throws may affect his next one. Missing might make him nervous, or scoring might give him confidence.

parts.q: The table below shows the number of games in which Rohan scored each of the given number of points. For example, Rohan scored 12 points in 3 games. Work out Rohan’s mean number of points per game, based on the values in the table. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.scheme: $\mu = \frac{\sum fx}{\sum f} = \frac{4(0) + 5(6) + 4(8) + 2(10) + 3(12) + 1(16)}{4 + 5 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 1} = \frac{134}{19} = 7{\cdot}05263 = 7{\cdot}05$ points. Incorrect rounding: full credit −1.

idea.title: Mean from a frequency table
idea.text: Each column says "this score happened this many times". Multiply each score by how often it happened to get the total, then divide by the total number of games.

steps.say: Total points: multiply each number of points by the number of games, then add.
Total games: add the bottom row.
Mean = total points ÷ total games. Round to 2 decimal places: 7.05 points.

parts.tip: Divide by the number of games (19), not by the number of columns (6).

questions.topic: Pentagon spinner: angles and area, sample space, probability and a fair game
questions.stem: A toy company makes spinners in the shape of a regular pentagon, as shown in the diagram on the right (not to scale). Each of the five sides of the pentagon $ABCDE$ is the same length. The pentagon is divided into five congruent isosceles triangles. Each triangle contains the point $O$. $|\angle BOC| = 72^\circ$ and $|AO| = 6$ cm.
questions.fig: A regular pentagon ABCDE split into five isosceles triangles that meet at the centre O, with |AO| = 6 cm and the angle BOC = 72° marked. Part (c) shows the spinner with its five triangles numbered 1 to 5. Part (d) has a table of outcomes N, S, E, W with their probabilities and prizes.

parts.q: Work out $|\angle CBA|$, the size of the angle $CBA$.

idea.title: Isosceles triangles
idea.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, and the two angles opposite them are equal. The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°.

steps.say: In triangle BOC, |OB| = |OC| (both go from the centre to a corner), so it's isosceles and its two base angles are equal.
The angles of a triangle add to 180°. Take away the 72° and share the rest equally.
At B, the angle CBA is made of two of these base angles: ∠OBC (from triangle BOC) and ∠OBA (from triangle AOB, which is congruent). So the angle is 108°.

parts.q: Work out the area of the triangle $AOB$, and hence work out the area of the pentagon $ABCDE$. Give each answer correct to 1 decimal place. (You do not need to use your answer from part (a).)

answer.show: Area of triangle AOB = 17.1 cm², area of pentagon = 85.6 cm²

parts.scheme: Area $\triangle = \frac12(6)(6)\sin 72^\circ = 17{\cdot}119 = 17{\cdot}1$ cm². Area of pentagon $= 17{\cdot}119 \times 5 = 85{\cdot}59... = 85{\cdot}6$ cm². (Calculator in radians gives 4·56 and 22·84.)

idea.title: Area of a triangle from two sides and an angle
idea.text: If you know two sides and the angle between them: Area = ½ab sin C. It's in the Formulae and Tables booklet.

steps.say: |OA| = |OB| = 6 cm, because every corner is 6 cm from O. The angle AOB is 72°, the same as all five angles at the centre.
Use Area = ½ab sin C with the two 6 cm sides and the 72° angle between them.
The pentagon is 5 of these triangles. Multiply the unrounded value, then round: 85.6 cm².

parts.tip: Your calculator must be in degrees (DEG). In radians you would get 4.56.

parts.q: The triangles in the spinner are numbered 1 to 5, as shown. The spinner is spun twice, and each number landed on is recorded. Write down a sample space to show all of the 25 possible outcomes when the spinner is spun twice. It may be useful to draw a two-way table or to list the outcomes in a systematic way.
parts.scheme: Two-way table of pairs (1,1) to (5,5), or a tree diagram, or some other acceptable list of outcomes. 15 elements correct: high partial credit.

idea.title: Sample space
idea.text: The sample space is the list of every possible outcome. For two spins, each outcome is a pair (first spin, second spin). A two-way table makes sure none are missed.

steps.say: Put the first spin down the side (1 to 5) and the second spin across the top (1 to 5).
Each cell is the pair (first spin, second spin). 5 rows × 5 columns gives all 25 outcomes.

parts.q: The spinner is spun twice, and the two numbers are added. What are the maximum and minimum possible totals when two numbers from the spinner are added?

steps.say: The biggest total comes from landing on the biggest number, 5, both times.
The smallest total comes from landing on 1 both times. So the maximum is 10 and the minimum is 2.

parts.q: Each time the spinner is spun, each number (1 to 5) is equally likely. Work out the probability of getting a total of either 4 or 5, when the two numbers are added.

idea.title: Probability of an event
idea.text: When every outcome is equally likely, P(event) = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes. A probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

steps.say: Write the total in every cell. A total of 4 comes up 3 times: (1,3), (2,2), (3,1). A total of 5 comes up 4 times: (1,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1).
Add the counts and divide by the 25 equally likely outcomes. The probability is 7/25.

parts.q: In a different spinner, there are 4 different outcomes: N, S, E, or W. In a game, Jena pays €1 to spin this spinner. The table below shows the probability of each outcome, as well as the money Jena will get, depending on the outcome. Is this game fair? Justify your answer. Work out the expected value of this game as part of your solution.

answer.show: E(x) = €0.90. Not fair: on average Jena gets back €0.90, less than the €1 she pays.

parts.scheme: $E(x) = \sum xP(x) = 1(0{\cdot}3) + 0{\cdot}5(0{\cdot}2) + 0(0{\cdot}4) + 5(0{\cdot}1) = €0{\cdot}90$. Not a fair game, as it costs €1 to play and the expected outcome €0·90 is less than the amount paid (or: expected value not equal to zero). Conclusion or explanation missing: full credit −1.

idea.title: Fair games
idea.text: A game is fair if, on average, you get back exactly what you pay to play. Work out the expected value (the average money back per go) and compare it with the cost.

steps.say: Multiply each amount of money by its probability.
Add them up: the expected value is €0.90.
Compare with the €1 she pays. On average Jena gets back 90c for every €1, so she loses 10c a go. The game is not fair.

parts.tip: Give the expected value AND the conclusion with its reason: leaving either out costs a mark.

questions.topic: Cards: listing outcomes and probability without replacement
questions.stem: Seán is playing a game with 14 cards. 7 of the cards are green (G), numbered 1 to 7. The other 7 cards are red (R), also numbered 1 to 7.
questions.fig: A two-way table with Number (1 to 7) across the top and Colour (Green (G), Red (R)) down the side; only G2 and R5 are filled in.

parts.q: Complete the table below to show all possible outcomes when a card is chosen. Some have already been completed for you. For example, G2 means the green card with the number 2.

answer.show: Green row: G1 G2 G3 G4 G5 G6 G7. Red row: R1 R2 R3 R4 R5 R6 R7.

parts.scheme: G1 to G7 in the green row and R1 to R7 in the red row. 7 or more correct: high partial credit.

idea.title: Listing outcomes
idea.text: Go through the outcomes in a fixed order so none are missed: colour first, then number 1 to 7.

steps.say: Each cell is the colour letter followed by the number at the top of its column.
Fill both rows. 2 colours × 7 numbers = 14 outcomes: one for each card.

parts.q: A card is chosen at random. Work out the probability of getting a card with an even number.

idea.title: Probability of an event
idea.text: When every outcome is equally likely, P(event) = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes. A probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

steps.say: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, in both colours: G2, G4, G6, R2, R4, R6. That's 6 cards.
Divide by the 14 cards. The probability is 3/7.

parts.q: Seán picks a card at random and doesn’t replace it. It is Red 5 (R5). He then picks a second card at random. What is the probability that the second card is a green card?
parts.scheme: (c) $\frac{7}{13}$; (d) $\frac{6}{13}$. One part correct: mid partial credit.

idea.title: Without replacement
idea.text: If a card is not put back, the second pick is from one fewer card. Count what is left before you work out the second probability.

steps.say: R5 is not put back, so 13 cards are left.
No green card was taken, so all 7 greens are still there. The probability is 7/13.

parts.q: Seán puts back the two cards. Seán picks a card at random and doesn’t replace it. He then picks a second card at random. Find the probability that the second card is a different colour and a different number from the first card.

steps.say: Whatever the first card is, the count works the same way. Say it is G3. Then 13 cards are left.
A different colour means one of the 7 red cards. A different number too means not R3. That leaves 6 cards.
So the probability is 6 out of the 13 cards left: 6/13.

questions.topic: Sleep: the empirical rule and independent nights
questions.fig: A normal curve for hours of sleep with the middle 68% shaded between 7·2 and 8·4. There are three empty boxes on the horizontal axis: one further left than 7·2, one in the middle, and one further right than 8·4.

parts.q: A large group of 17-year-olds were asked how many hours of sleep they got on the previous night. The results were normally distributed. The middle 68% slept between 7·2 and 8·4 hours, as shown on the diagram below. Use the empirical rule to answer parts (a)(i) and (a)(ii). Fill in the three missing numbers on the horizontal axis.

idea.title: The empirical rule
idea.text: For normally distributed data: about 68% lies within 1 standard deviation (σ) of the mean, 95% within 2σ, and 99·7% within 3σ. The mean is in the middle.

steps.say: The middle 68% is from one standard deviation below the mean to one above. So the mean is halfway between 7.2 and 8.4.
From 7.2 to 8.4 is two standard deviations.
The outer boxes are two standard deviations from the mean (2 × 0.6 = 1.2).

parts.q: Research says that a 17-year-old should get at least 9 hours of sleep each night. What percentage of this sample got at least 9 hours of sleep on the previous night?

steps.say: 9 hours is μ + 2σ. 95% of the group is between 6.6 and 9.0 hours.
The other 5% is split equally between the two ends: 2.5% below 6.6 and 2.5% above 9.0. So 2.5% got at least 9 hours.

parts.tip: Only the top end counts here, so halve the 5%.

parts.q: Owen records the number of hours of sleep that he gets each night for several weeks. Based on this, he calculates that he gets the recommended amount of sleep 10% of the time. What is the probability that he does not get the recommended amount of sleep on a particular night?
parts.scheme: (i) $1 - 0{\cdot}1 = 0{\cdot}9$ or 90%. (ii) $(0{\cdot}9)(0{\cdot}9)(0{\cdot}1) = 0{\cdot}081$ or 8·1%. One part correct: mid partial credit.

idea.title: The "not" rule
idea.text: Something either happens or it doesn't, so the two probabilities add up to 1. P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

steps.say: Owen's 10% comes from his own records (a relative frequency). As a decimal, that is his chance of enough sleep on a night.
Either he gets enough sleep or he doesn't, so subtract from 1. The probability is 0.9.

parts.q: Beginning on a Sunday night, Owen records his sleep each night for a week. Find the probability that Owen gets the recommended amount of sleep for the first time on Tuesday night (the third night). Assume that the number of hours of sleep Owen gets on different nights are independent.

idea.title: Independent events: multiply
idea.text: Independent means one result does not change the chances of the next. Then the chance of a whole list of results is the single chances multiplied together.

steps.say: First time on Tuesday means: Sunday not enough, Monday not enough, Tuesday enough.
The nights are independent, so multiply. The probability is 0.081.

questions.topic: Ice cream van: counting choices, Venn diagram, expected value and a sector logo
questions.stem: Diarmuid owns an ice cream van.
questions.fig: Part (b): a Venn diagram U (100) with circles V (42) and C (37) and 45 outside. Part (c): a table of typical sales and the probability of each weather condition. Part (d): an ice cream cone logo: a sector of radius 20 cm with angle θ at the centre, sitting on two right-angled triangles that meet at the bottom point; the two angles at the centre next to the dotted line are 70° and 70°, and the slanted side is l.

parts.q: Diarmuid sells: • 7 different flavours of ice cream • 4 different toppings • 2 containers: a choice of a cone or a tub. How many different choices are available if you must choose only one flavour, one topping, and either a cone or a tub?

idea.title: The fundamental principle of counting
idea.text: If you make several choices one after another, multiply the number of options for each choice. Every option for the first choice can go with every option for the second.

steps.say: Three choices in a row: a flavour (7 options), a topping (4 options) and a container (2 options).
Multiply. There are 56 different choices.

parts.q: Diarmuid wants to maximise the number of choices available to his customers. He can only add either an extra flavour or an extra topping. Should he add an extra flavour or an extra topping? Use calculations to support your answer.
parts.scheme: Extra topping: $7 \times 5 \times 2 = 70$, better than extra flavour: $8 \times 4 \times 2 = 64$. Correct box ticked but no justification: low partial credit; correct work but no or incorrect conclusion: full credit −1.

steps.say: Work out the number of choices both ways.
70 is more than 64, so he should add an extra topping.

parts.tip: Adding one to the smaller number (4 toppings) makes the bigger difference.

parts.q: One day, Diarmuid recorded the ice cream choices of the first 100 customers. • Vanilla ($V$) flavour was bought by 42 customers. • A cone ($C$) was bought by 37 customers. • 45 customers bought neither vanilla nor a cone. This information is shown in the Venn diagram below. Complete the Venn diagram below, to show the number of customers in each region.

answer.show: V only 18, V and C 24, C only 13 (45 outside)

parts.scheme: Bought vanilla and a cone $= 42 + 37 - 55 = 24$ people; V only 18, C only 13, 45 outside. Accept correct values without work. (100 − 45, or 79, 24, 124 written: partial credit.)

idea.title: Venn diagrams
idea.text: Each region of a Venn diagram is a different group: in A only, in both, in B only, and in neither (outside the circles but inside the box). Every person is in exactly one region, so all the regions add up to the total.

steps.say: 45 are outside both circles, so the rest are inside at least one circle.
Adding V and C counts the overlap twice: 42 + 37 = 79. That is 79 − 55 = 24 too many, so 24 people are in both.
Vanilla only = 42 − 24. Cone only = 37 − 24.
Check: all four regions add to 100.

parts.q: A customer is picked at random from the first 100 customers. Find the probability that this customer bought a cone with a flavour other than vanilla.

idea.title: Probability of an event
idea.text: When every outcome is equally likely, P(event) = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes. A probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

steps.say: A cone but not vanilla is the cone-only part of the diagram: 13 customers.
Divide by 100. The probability is 13/100 = 0.13.

parts.q: In general, sales of ice creams increase as weather conditions improve. Diarmuid’s typical ice cream sales for different weather conditions are shown in the table below. The table also shows the probability of each weather condition next Sunday. Use the information in the table to work out the expected value of Diarmuid’s ice cream sales next Sunday.

idea.title: Expected value
idea.text: The expected value is the average result per go if you played many, many times. Multiply each result by its probability, then add them all up: E(x) = Σ x·P(x).

steps.say: Change the percentages to decimals: 30% = 0.3, 45% = 0.45 and 25% = 0.25.
Multiply each sales figure by its probability and add. The expected sales are €247.50.

parts.q: Diarmuid has a logo of an ice cream cone on the side of his van. The logo is made up of a sector of a circle with radius 20 cm, and two identical right-angled triangles, as shown in the diagram (not to scale). The arc of the sector is labelled $s$. The sizes of some of the angles are shown. Find the size of the angle $\theta$ and hence, find the length of the arc $s$. Give the length in cm, correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.scheme: $\theta = 360 - 2(70) = 220^\circ$; arc length $= \frac{220}{360}[2\pi(20)] = 76{\cdot}79... = 76{\cdot}8$ cm. Accept answers without units; no or incorrect rounding: full credit −1.

idea.title: Arc length
idea.text: An arc is a fraction of the circle's circumference. The fraction is the angle at the centre over 360°: arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.

steps.say: The angles all the way round the centre add to 360°. The two 70° angles belong to the triangles, so θ is the rest.
The arc is 220/360 of the whole circumference, 2π(20). Round to 1 decimal place: 76.8 cm.

parts.q: Use trigonometry to work out the length of the side labelled $l$. Give your answer correct to the nearest cm.
parts.scheme: $\tan 70^\circ = \frac{l}{20}$, $l = 20\tan 70^\circ = 55$ cm. No or incorrect rounding: full credit −1.

idea.title: Tan in a right-angled triangle
idea.text: tan (angle) = opposite ÷ adjacent. Use it when you know one of those two sides and want the other.

steps.say: Look at one right-angled triangle. The 70° angle is at the centre. The 20 cm radius is next to it (adjacent) and l is opposite it.
Opposite and adjacent means use tan. Round to the nearest cm: 55 cm.

questions.topic: Tennis tree diagram, first loss on the third game, spheres and expected goals
questions.fig: A tree diagram for two matches: Match 1 (Win 0·6, Lose box empty), then Match 2 (after Win: Win 0·7, Lose box empty; after Lose: Win box empty, Lose 0·3), and a Probability column with 0·42 for Win-Win and 0·12 for Lose-Lose (the other two empty). Part (d): a table of shot probabilities and numbers of shots.

head: Probability of resulting in a goal

parts.q: Seán is playing two tennis matches. He either wins or loses each match. The probability that he wins the first match is 0·6 and the probability that he wins the second match is 0·7. The outcomes of the two matches are independent. Use this information above to complete the tree diagram below, by: writing the probability associated with each branch of the tree diagram into the appropriate box and

answer.show: Match 1 Lose: 0.4. Match 2 after a Win: Lose 0.3. Match 2 after a Loss: Win 0.7.

parts.scheme: Branches: Match 1 Lose 0·4; after Win, Lose 0·3; after Lose, Win 0·7. Outcomes: WW 0·42, WL 0·18, LW 0·28, LL 0·12. Four entries correct: high partial credit.

idea.title: Tree diagrams
idea.text: A tree shows events happening one after another. Each branch is one possible result, labelled with its probability. The branches from one point add up to 1. Multiply along a path to get the chance of that path; add paths when more than one path fits.

steps.say: He either wins or loses, so the two branches from any point add to 1.
The matches are independent, so match 2 has the same chances whatever happened in match 1: Win 0.7, Lose 0.3.

parts.q: working out the probability for each outcome and writing it in the appropriate box in the final column.
parts.scheme: Win-Lose $0{\cdot}18$ and Lose-Win $0{\cdot}28$ (with the given 0·42 and 0·12).

steps.say: Multiply along each path. The two given boxes check the method: 0.6 × 0.7 = 0.42 and 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12.
Check: the four outcomes add to 1.

parts.q: Based on the tree diagram, what is the probability that Seán wins at least 1 match?

steps.say: At least 1 win covers every outcome except losing both matches.
So subtract Lose-Lose from 1. The probability is 0.88.

parts.q: Sarah also plays tennis. Each time that Sarah plays a service game, the probability that she wins is 0·78. Assume that winning each service game is independent. What is the probability that Sarah will lose her next service game (that is, that she won’t win her next service game)?
parts.scheme: (i) $P(SL) = 1 - 0{\cdot}78 = 0{\cdot}22$. (ii) $P(W, W, L) = 0{\cdot}78 \times 0{\cdot}78 \times 0{\cdot}22 = 0{\cdot}133848 = 0{\cdot}134$. One part correct: mid partial credit.

idea.title: The "not" rule
idea.text: Something either happens or it doesn't, so the two probabilities add up to 1. P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

steps.say: Each service game she either wins or loses, so the two probabilities add to 1.
Subtract 0.78 from 1. The probability she loses is 0.22.

parts.q: What is the probability that the first service game that Sarah loses is her third service game? Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
parts.scheme: $0{\cdot}78 \times 0{\cdot}78 \times 0{\cdot}22 = 0{\cdot}133848 = 0{\cdot}134$. No or incorrect rounding: full credit −1.

idea.title: Independent events: multiply
idea.text: Independent means one result does not change the chances of the next. Then the chance of a whole list of results is the single chances multiplied together.

steps.say: First loss on the third game means: win, win, lose.
The games are independent, so multiply. Round to 3 decimal places: 0.134.

parts.q: A child’s football is in the shape of a sphere and has a diameter of 18 cm. Find the volume of this ball. Give your answer, in cm³, in terms of $\pi$.
parts.scheme: $V = \frac43\pi(9)^3 = 972\pi$ cm³. Answer not in terms of π: full credit −1.

idea.title: Volume of a sphere
idea.text: V = (4/3)πr³ (it's in the Formulae and Tables booklet). You need the radius, which is half the diameter.

steps.say: The radius is half the diameter: 18 ÷ 2 = 9 cm.
Use V = (4/3)πr³ and leave π in the answer. The volume is 972π cm³.

parts.tip: "In terms of π" means leave the π as a letter: don't multiply it out.

parts.q: An adult’s football is in the shape of a sphere and has a volume of 5424·6 cm³. Work out the radius of the adult’s football. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.scheme: $V = \frac43\pi r^3 = 5424{\cdot}6$; $r^3 = 1295{\cdot}027...$; $r = 10{\cdot}899... = 10{\cdot}9$ cm. No or incorrect rounding, or no units: full credit −1.

steps.say: Put the volume into the formula.
Get r³ on its own: divide both sides by (4/3)π.
Take the cube root and round to 1 decimal place. The radius is 10.9 cm.

parts.q: The Expected Goals (xG) is a method used to measure the probability that a particular type of shot will result in a goal. During a game, a team had 15 shots on goal. The statistician gave each shot a probability of resulting in a goal, as shown in the table below. Use the information in the table to work out the Expected Goals of the team in this game, that is, the expected value of the number of goals that would be scored from these 15 shots.

idea.title: Expected value
idea.text: The expected value is the average result per go if you played many, many times. Multiply each result by its probability, then add them all up: E(x) = Σ x·P(x).

steps.say: Each shot is worth its probability in expected goals. 6 shots at 10% are worth 6 × 0.1 goals, and so on. Change the percentages to decimals first.
Multiply and add. The Expected Goals is 3.5.
